The product distance reduces to |t-u| for the unique R^0 coordinate.

background_notes.justification: For every t,u the displayed product distance equals |t-u|; taking suprema proves diameter preservation. Images commute with unions and remain countably indexed, so each admissible cover pushes to an admissible cover of F with identical cost. background_notes.fact: For a family of nonnegative extended-real costs with infimum zero, every eta>0 admits a member of cost <eta. A countable cover can be indexed by N, padding a finite cover by empty sets at zero cost.

The content is the infimum of costs of countable covers, with empty members costing zero.

Enumerating a countable family, or padding a finite one, gives the sequence used in F001 without changing coverage or cost.

background_notes.fact: A nonempty zero-diameter Euclidean set is a singleton. In R^n with n≥1, an open ball of radius b/2 for b>0 contains its center and has diameter b. For q>0 the declared beta_i is positive, beta_i≤r/2, and beta_i^q≤epsilon*2^(-i-3).

grounds.reason: The branch has n≥1 and q,r,epsilon>0.
beta_i is the minimum of r/2 and the positive q-th root of epsilon*2^(-i-3).

background_notes.justification: Distance zero forces any two points of a zero-diameter set to coincide. The triangle inequality gives ball diameter ≤b; points tending to opposite ends along any coordinate axis give distances tending to b, hence equality of the supremum. Positive real powers are increasing on nonnegative reals, and the positive q-th root has q-th power equal to its argument. These facts establish all replacement guards and costs.

background_notes.fact: For epsilon>0, sum_(i≥0) epsilon*2^(-i-3)=epsilon/4. Nonnegative countable sums are monotone under termwise domination and restriction of indices, and are additive for termwise sums and homogeneous for finite nonnegative scalars.

grounds.reason: Each singleton replacement adds a nonnegative cost at most epsilon*2^(-i-3); the other members are unchanged.

background_notes.justification: The finite geometric sum is (epsilon/4)(1-2^(-M-1)) for indices 0 through M, whose supremum is epsilon/4. Defining nonnegative series by suprema of finite partial sums proves monotonicity and scalar multiplication; additivity follows by taking common finite index supersets. Consequently the new total is at most the old total plus epsilon/4, hence strictly below epsilon.

background_notes.fact: For each i in countable K, finitely many intervals indexed by 1≤j≤N_i give a countable family of products. If diam(U_i)=r_i and each interval has length ≤r_i, each product has Euclidean diameter ≤sqrt(2)r_i. For r_i>0 and q>0, N_i≤2/r_i implies N_i(sqrt(2)r_i)^(q+1)≤2(sqrt(2))^(q+1)r_i^q, also after nonnegative summation.

For points in a fixed product both coordinate distances are ≤r_i, and the product distance is therefore ≤sqrt(2)r_i. Monotonicity of positive real powers bounds each cost. The usual real-power laws for positive factors give the displayed termwise identity and inequality; taking suprema of finite subsums yields the series estimate.
